http://www.euronews.com/2026/07/29/iraq-.text: Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan said on Tuesday that Iraq had offered to supply Turkey with up to 1 million barrels of oil a day as Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Zeydi visited Ankara for talks on energy and regional security."Our neighbour is right here," Erdoğan said at a joint press conference following talks at the presidential complex. "Our goal now is to sign a comprehensive energy cooperation agreement as soon as possible that will benefit both sides.""Once we transfer 1 million barrels of oil from our neighbour Iraq, it will meet our needs," the Turkish president said. Zeydi confirmed the figure, adding, "Yes, that is correct, 1 million."No binding agreement on the volume or timeline was signed on Tuesday. However, the two sides signed a deal for Turkish Petroleum to acquire a 15% stake in BP's operations at the Kirkuk oilfield, with Erdoğan calling it "a historic step" as the broader energy cooperation agreement is still being negotiated.Turkey imports around 90% of its oil and has been under pressure to diversify its supply since the outbreak of the Iran war, which pushed up global energy prices and closed the Strait of Hormuz. Iraq is already one of its closest trading partners and a major source of crude.Zeydi chose Ankara for his third overseas visit after Washington and Tehran. The two leaders also discussed issues in the broader region, including Palestine, Syria and Iran. Erdoğan said Turkey was ready to supply Iraq with defence equipment.Development Road and other projects on the tableThe $17 billion Development Road — a motorway, railway and pipeline corridor running roughly 1,200 kilometres from Iraq's port of Basra to the Turkish border and onward to Europe — was a key part of the talks.Zeydi said work had gained new momentum. Transport Minister Abdülkadir Uraloğlu said the two sides were close to finalising details and that construction could begin before the end of 2026.The project was first announced in 2023 and is designed to give Iraq a direct land route to European markets, reducing its dependence on Gulf shipping. The goal has become more pressing since the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.The decades-old Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline agreement expired in July 2026. The two countries are negotiating a replacement deal, which Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said must include a mechanism guaranteeing full use of the pipeline's capacity of up to 1.5 million barrels per day.The pipeline had been shut since March 2023 following an arbitration ruling against Turkey over Kurdish oil exports. Reviving it has been a priority for both governments.Bayraktar said Turkey was also examining ways to send natural gas to Iraqi power plants struggling with shortages.On water, the two countries signed a new framework for managing the shared Euphrates and Tigris river system, due to take effect on 1 September.Joint infrastructure projects will be funded from a dedicated account drawing on Iraqi oil revenues from sales to Turkey, with Turkish companies leading construction.Water has been a long-running source of tension between the two countries: Iraq has repeatedly complained that Turkish dams upstream have reduced downstream flows to critically low levels.

Photograph: Lasse Bak Mejlvang/Netflix/Courtesy of Netflix Movies Review The Secret Woman review – Claes Bang is dastardly gaslighter in Danish amnesia thriller In spite of capable performances and deployment of hygge , gothic and Nordic noir elements, you’ll search for a feasible plot or a character insight in vain Phil Hoad Fri 28 Aug 2026 02.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 28 Aug 2026 02.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A dapted from the 2017 novel by Anna Ekberg (actually a male writing duo), this thriller from Denmark chucks in a bit of everything into the mix: hygge lakeside melodrama, manor-house gothic, and Nordic-noir corruption. But this franticness can’t disguise that it’s a dopey and facile thriller that, despite capable performances, plumbs neither its characters’ depths nor hits thematic pay dirt. It also merits a stiff investigation from the plotting police. Despite amnesia that leaves her unable to remember her life prior to running an idyllic Norwegian rural cafe, Louise (Natalie Wolfsberg Madueño) is gearing up to get hitched to crime writer Joachim (Pål Sverre Hagen). When a tourist approaches and calls her by another name, she is sufficiently shaken to take a DNA test; it confirms she is actually Helene Söderberg, a Danish shipping heiress presumed dead, with a husband and son back home. Originally found stowed away on a cargo ship, she handed over an ID card – for Louise Anderson – which the authorities accepted. Now wanting to reclaim her identity, she pitches up on the capacious doorstep of company executive Edmund (Claes Bang), her former partner. Frankly, it doesn’t seem credible that Helene would have remained incurious about her past for that long – especially given her blackout was so total. And director Barbara Topsøe-Rothenborg leads her forward in further implausible style, as she tiptoes around the hallways of her previous moneyed existence, while back in Norway, Joachim wears out Google looking for the truth. There are too many slack and over-convenient revelations, such as the yearbook with ripped-out pages carelessly left around by a conglomerate that has successfully laundered its dirty linen online. Helene’s memory, meanwhile, seems to exclusively recover at moments screaming for further exposition. With Edmund’s dastardliness confirmed early, his gaslighting is largely robbed of the required psychological tension, however much Topsøe-Rothenborg windmill-tilts the hell out of everything going on under his gothic roof. She prefers to stick with easy shorthand, such as his Mrs Danvers-like mother (Stina Ekblad) hovering at the top of stairways, rather than meaningfully explore Edmund’s damaged psyche, or offer more than expedient engagement with the topic of human trafficking, on which everything hangs here. Madueño is a sympathetic lead, and Bang cannily uses mildness as cover for extreme anger. But they are undermined by a scatty plot that won’t be worrying Stieg Larsson or Jo Nesbø any time soon. News 1 d ago Despite thefts and errors, Lithuanian retailers are embracing self-checkout News 1 d ago airBaltic to halve direct routes from Lithuania next summer News 1 d ago Russian deputy foreign minister says Moscow has no plans to attack Baltics News 1 d ago New evidence links Teltonika devices to Russia as Lithuaniaâs export control system stalls News 1 d ago Lithuania election official faces ethics scrutiny over reported ties to political party News 1 d ago Lithuania warns citizens against travel to Belarus after Lithuanian tour organiser jailed News 1 d ago Latvia, Estonia issue airspace warnings after drones approach borders News 1 d ago War on words: Russia destroyed a third of Ukraineâs annual book production this summer News 2026.08.20 08:00 Green commitments, fossil temptations: Lithuaniaâs Baltic oil dilemma IJ Irma JanauskaitÄ, LRT TV, LRT.lt 2026.08.20 08:00 Oil extraction. | Shutterstock Lithuania's government has ruled out offshore oil drilling in the Baltic Sea as part of its commitment to phasing out fossil fuels â even as Russia's Lukoil pumps oil from fields just kilometres from the Lithuanian coast, and geologists warn that domestic onshore reserves will be exhausted within a few years.Â A quarter of a century ago, Lithuania had a thriving oil industry. Today it is on its last legs, and geologists say what remains onshore will be exhausted within a few years. The question now dividing the industry, politicians and environmentalists is whether Lithuania should look to the Baltic Sea â where Russia is already pumping oil from fields that may, some geologists suspect, connect directly to deposits on the Lithuanian side. Almost empty The SakuÄiai field, one of several operated by Minijos Nafta, one of Lithuania's largest oil producers, has been pumping since 2002. Output has fallen from nearly 600,000 cubic metres at its peak in 2001 to just 26,000 last year. The company can still extract oil from five fields in total, but has shut down two â nearly empty â and was blocked by courts from opening a new site at Kintai. "Explored and exploited onshore deposits are naturally running out, despite the industry's efforts to extract the last drop," said geologist Jonas SatkÅ«nas. The story of Minijos Nafta mirrors the wider arc of Lithuanian oil: a brief boom, a peak, and a long decline. Just across the water Geologists say the real prize was never onshore. Beneath the Baltic Sea, they argue, lie deposits comparable in scale to those already being exploited on the Russian side â and Russia's Lukoil is making full use of them. Baltic sea | D. Umbrasas / LRT The company has been pumping oil from the Baltic seabed near Lithuania for years, from a field roughly 20 kilometres from the Curonian Spit â the narrow strip of land that separates the Baltic sea from the Curonian Lagoon and forms part of Lithuania's coastline. It is now expanding to a new site around 50 kilometres offshore, where one field alone is estimated to hold 20 million tonnes of oil. "There are grounds to believe the Baltic Sea holds oil resources equivalent to â possibly even greater than â what has been found and is being exploited on the Russian side, in the same water, in the same sea," SatkÅ«nas said. Jonas SatkÅ«nas | LRT still frame Some geologists go further, suggesting the two fields may be connected underground â raising the pointed question of whether Lithuanian oil is already flowing across to the Russian side. Ignas VaiÄeliÅ«nas, production director at Minijos Nafta, put it in blunt terms: "If there are half a million tonnes out there, that's a quarter of Lithuania's own annual consumption. If we dared to go offshore, we could have those same volumes." The industry argues that offshore production would cost the state nothing â exploration and extraction costs would fall to private companies â while generating significant tax revenues. It would also reduce the distance oil needs to be transported to the Orlen refinery at MaÅ¾eikiai in northern Lithuania, currently the only oil refinery in the Baltic states. Political headwinds But Lithuania's government isn't interested, at least for now. The country has committed to phasing out fossil fuels as part of its green transition, and the environment ministry shows no sign of changing course. "The strategic direction set out in the government programme is oriented towards green transformation, the development of renewable energy and the protection of ecosystems," said deputy environment minister GiedrÄ RiÄkutÄ. Oil extraction | AP The oil industry points out that fuel consumption in Lithuania is actually rising, not falling, undermining the case for leaving domestic resources untapped on environmental grounds. If the country is going to use the oil anyway, the argument goes, it might as well produce some of it itself. The political sensitivity of offshore drilling is not unique to Lithuania. Last year a Canadian company operating in Poland announced the discovery of what it called one of the largest oil finds in Europe in a decade, in the Baltic Sea near the port city of ÅwinoujÅcie â a find it described as historic for Poland's energy sector. The announcement was almost immediately followed by protests from German environmental groups opposed to a test drilling operation, and the dispute has been intensifying since. Lithuania's own history with the industry is similarly charged: previous attempts to bring in foreign investment, including a proposal involving US energy giant Chevron, were rejected amid public opposition.
